definition: The finding that for a fixed compute budget, model size and training tokens should scale together (roughly 20 tokens per parameter under original assumptions).
details: The finding that for a fixed compute budget, model size and training tokens should scale together (roughly 20 tokens per parameter under original assumptions). Earlier models were undertrained on data; Chinchilla reset the recipe.

explainer.lead: Compute-optimal training is a way to decide how large a language model should be and how much text it should train on when computing resources are fixed. Known as Chinchilla, it showed that spending the whole budget on a bigger model can be worse than training a smaller one on more data.

tiers.eli5: Imagine you have a fixed amount of time to study for a test. Building a huge set of notes is not helpful if you never have time to read them, so you need a balance between how many notes you make and how long you spend studying them. Chinchilla gives the same kind of advice for training language models: balance the model’s size with the amount of training text.
tiers.practitioner: When planning pretraining under a fixed compute budget, choose parameter count and training-token count together rather than maximizing either one alone. The original Chinchilla assumptions give a rough starting point of 20 tokens per parameter, but the ratio should not be treated as assumption-free or universal.
tiers.paperLevel: For a fixed compute budget, compute-optimal training selects parameter count N and training-token count D so that both scale together; under the original Chinchilla assumptions, this gives D approximately 20N. Its central conclusion is that earlier models were undertrained on data. The numerical ratio is tied to those original assumptions rather than being an unconditional constant.

explainer.example: Under the original rough rule, a model with 1 billion parameters would be paired with about 20 billion training tokens. If the same fixed budget were spent mainly on adding parameters, the larger model could end up undertrained.

usedIn.name: Large language model pretraining
usedIn.detail: Guides the balance between parameter count and training-token count.

usedIn.name: Fixed-budget training planning
usedIn.detail: Helps allocate limited computation between a larger model and more training data.

explainer.intuition: A model cannot benefit from extra parameters if it sees too little training data. With limited compute, a smaller, better-trained model can therefore be a better choice than a larger, undertrained one.
howItWorks: Start with the fixed compute budget.
Treat model size and training tokens as linked choices.
Scale both together instead of maximizing model size alone.
Under the original assumptions, aim for roughly 20 tokens per parameter.
explainer.whyItMatters: Chinchilla reset the training recipe by showing that earlier models were undertrained on data. It makes training-data quantity a first-order design decision alongside model size.
misconceptions: Bigger is not automatically better under a fixed compute budget.
The 20-to-1 ratio is a rough result under original assumptions, not a universal law.
Compute-optimal training concerns both model size and tokens, not data quantity alone.
